comments.content: `@types/bun` and `bun-types` are two alternative providers of the same global Bun/JSX type definitions (`@types/bun` even depends on `bun-types`, as seen in `bun.lock`). Declaring both is redundant, and if the `types` scope in `tsconfig.json` is ever removed, both would be auto-included and produce duplicate-identifier errors. `tsconfig.json` already scopes `"types": ["bun-types"]`, so `@types/bun` is effectively unused. Keep a single provider and align `tsconfig.json` with it.

Fix: always select `rowid` (use the `SELECT rowid AS "__jm_rowid", *` form for both branches) and treat a NULL key as absent so it falls back to the unique rowid.

In a long-lived process (`jm serve`, repeated ingests) these descriptors accumulate. Keep a reference to the stream and destroy it in the `finally` (e.g. `const input = createReadStream(...)` then `} finally { rl.close(); input.destroy(); }`).

comments.content: The operator group is matched left-to-right and the trailing `(.+)` absorbs whatever follows, so an unsupported operator whose prefix matches a supported one is silently accepted instead of rejected. For example `size <> 5` parses as `col=size, op=">", rawVal="< 5"` → SQL `f.size > '< 5'`; comparing an INTEGER column against a text literal is always true in SQLite, so the predicate is silently dropped and every row is returned instead of the intended `<>`. The same happens for `size === 5`. Note this also makes the `OPS` guard ineffective here — the op is already `>`/`=`, so `JM_WHERE_OP` can never fire and the line is not "loud" as its comment claims. Require a non-operator character (or end-of-input) after the operator so unknown operators are rejected loudly, and add `<>` to both this regex and `OPS` if it should be supported.

comments.content: `res.usageMissing` is ignored here, unlike the sibling judged verbs (`filter.ts`, `find.ts`, `decision-tree.ts`), which all throw `JM_JUDGE_USAGE_MISSING` after `judge.ask()`. When the response carries no `usage` block the client returns `costUsd: 0` as a placeholder, so those calls are counted as free and `costPerCall`/`costUsdTotal` silently understate the run's cost. Since `evaluate` is a measurement verb, a fabricated $0 in its cost metric is exactly the failure mode D-046 guards against. Either throw on `usageMissing` (matching the other verbs) or exclude such cases from the cost aggregates and surface the count.
